opus-5.5.text:
I think conjecture generation is one of the most interesting and least solved parts of the whole picture. When people talk about AI for math, they usually mean proving: you hand the system a well-posed statement and ask whether it can find a proof. That's hard, but it has a very clean signal. With a formal language like Lean, the proof either checks or it doesn't, so you can build a reinforcement learning loop around that verifier.

Conjecturing is different because there's no verifier for "this is a good question." A conjecture can be true and completely boring. It can be false in an instructive way. It can be technically open but nobody cares. What mathematicians value is a mix of things: does it unify phenomena that looked unrelated, does it point toward a deeper structure, is it the right level of difficulty, so it isn't trivial but you can imagine a path. That's a taste judgment, and taste is very hard to turn into a reward.

So I'd break the challenge into a few pieces.

The first is generation. Models are actually decent at producing plausible statements, sometimes too good, because they'll produce a thousand variations that are all slight perturbations of known theorems. The hard part is getting real novelty rather than surface recombination.

The second is filtering, and here you have tools. You can search for counterexamples computationally, check small cases, try to prove or disprove things in a formal system, and throw away whatever is false or falls immediately. That's where a strong prover feeds back into the conjecturer. If you have a system that can quickly dispose of easy statements, then whatever survives is more interesting by construction.

The third, and the hardest, is interestingness. One idea I find promising is measuring a conjecture by what it unlocks. If assuming it lets you prove many other things, or compresses a lot of existing results, that's a signal it's capturing structure. Mathematics has this self-referential quality where a good conjecture is one that organizes the landscape. You can try to approximate that with the dependency graph of a formal library.

Historically, a lot of great conjectures came from staring at data. Think of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer computing with elliptic curves, or the Ramanujan-style pattern spotting. AI is very good at patterns in large data, so in some areas where you can generate lots of examples, like combinatorics, number theory, or knot invariants, I think machines can genuinely suggest relationships humans wouldn't see.

My view is that the end state is a loop: a conjecturer proposes, a prover attacks, a verifier checks, and what comes out of that loop updates both sides. That's what self-improving mathematical intelligence would look like. Proving teaches you what's true, and conjecturing teaches you what's worth asking. You really need both to get something that looks like a mathematician rather than just a very fast problem solver.

r001.rationale: The response says a conjecturer and prover interact in a loop, with the results updating both sides, and describes this as self-improving mathematical intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think conjecture formulation is actually the harder half of the problem, and it's been underrated because proving is so much easier to measure. When you ask a model to prove something, you have a formal verifier like Lean that tells you yes or no. When you ask a model to conjecture, there's no oracle for "is this interesting?" That's the core research difficulty.

Let me break down what I think the challenge really consists of. First, there's taste. A true statement is cheap. You can generate infinitely many trivially true statements, and a system optimized naively will do exactly that. What a good mathematician does is find statements that sit at the boundary of what's known, that connect two areas that didn't seem related, or that, if true, would unlock a lot of downstream results. Encoding that sense of significance into a training signal is very hard, because it's a judgment that even human mathematicians disagree about and that shifts over decades.

Second, there's the data problem. The literature records theorems and proofs, but it almost never records the process of arriving at a conjecture. The failed guesses, the numerical experiments, the moment someone noticed a pattern in a table of values and thought, this can't be a coincidence. That reasoning is mostly invisible, so models learn from the polished output rather than the exploratory process. We have to reconstruct that process somehow, often by building environments where the model does the exploring itself.

Third, and this is where I think the field is most actively moving, is the loop between conjecture and verification. If you can formalize a candidate statement and attempt to prove or disprove it quickly, you get a feedback signal. Counterexamples are enormously informative. A conjecture that survives serious attempts to break it is more valuable than one that's never been tested. So the systems that will do this well are not pure generators. They're generator, critic, and prover working together, and the conjecture quality emerges from that interaction.

My honest view is that the near-term wins will come in areas where the search space is structured enough that the system can run experiments. Combinatorics, number theory, certain parts of analysis where you can compute. The deeper, more conceptual conjectures, the Langlands-type statements that reorganize an entire field, those require something closer to a new framework, and I don't think we have a clear path to that yet. But I also don't think it's impossible. The question I find most exciting is whether, with enough scale and the right environments, taste turns out to be learnable the way proof search turned out to be.

r001.rationale: The response describes a conjecture–verification feedback loop, says counterexamples are informative, and says conjecture quality emerges from generator, critic, and prover interaction. This communicates that interaction can improve the system’s conjecturing.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that formulating a conjecture requires more than recognizing a pattern. You can look at examples and propose a statement that fits all of them, but that doesn’t necessarily make it an interesting mathematical conjecture. It might be trivial, or it might fail as soon as you look beyond those examples.

So there are really two questions: Can AI generate plausible statements, and can it judge which statements are worth pursuing? The second seems much harder. What makes a conjecture valuable is often its relationship to other mathematics—whether it explains something, connects ideas, or opens up a useful direction.

I’d be interested in a system that works in a loop: generate examples, propose a conjecture, search for counterexamples, try to prove it, and revise it when something breaks. Even an unsuccessful proof attempt can reveal that you need a different hypothesis. Getting that interaction to work seems like a promising research direction, with mathematicians helping assess whether the resulting questions are actually meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes a system that proposes conjectures, tries to prove them, and revises them after failures, but it does not identify an AI prover interacting with an AI conjecturer or state that this interaction enables them to self-improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that formulating a conjecture is much less well-defined than proving one. If you give an AI a statement to prove, there’s a fairly clear notion of success. But if you ask it to propose a conjecture, what makes that conjecture good? It should be true, of course, but it should also be interesting, surprising, and connected to something mathematicians care about. A system could generate infinitely many true statements and still produce very little useful mathematics.

So part of the research challenge is getting AI to move between examples and abstractions: notice a pattern, formulate a precise statement, look for counterexamples, and revise it. But another part is developing mathematical taste—some ability to recognize which patterns are worth pursuing. I think that makes conjecture generation a particularly interesting setting for collaboration between mathematicians and AI, because checking a statement and judging its significance are quite different tasks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI conjecture generation and collaboration between mathematicians and AI, but it does not state that interaction between an AI conjecturer and an AI prover enables self-improvement.
